content: Vegetable oils can be used as fuel due to their properties being similar to diesel fuel, although they have higher viscosity and lower oxidative stability. To use vegetable oil as a substitute for 2 diesel fuel, particularly in engines or home heating systems, these differences must be addressed. For engines designed to burn 2 diesel fuel, the viscosity of vegetable oil must be reduced to ensure proper atomization during combustion. Failure to do so can result in incomplete combustion, carbon buildup, and eventual engine damage. Enthusiasts often refer to vegetable oil used as fuel as waste vegetable oil (WVO) if it is discarded oil from restaurants, or straight vegetable oil (SVO) to distinguish it from biodiesel. The first recorded use of vegetable oil as a fuel for a diesel engine occurred in 1900 when an engine built by the Otto company was demonstrated running on pure peanut oil at the World’s Fair. Later, Rudolf Diesel himself explored the use of vegetable oils as engine fuel and, in 1912, predicted their potential importance as alternatives to mineral oils. Research into vegetable oil as a diesel substitute has been spurred by periodic petroleum shortages, particularly during the 1930s, 1940s, 1970s, and early 1980s. The 1970s also saw the establishment of the first commercial enterprise, Elsbett of Germany, which enabled consumers to run their vehicles on straight vegetable oil. During the Bougainville conflict in the 1990s, islanders used coconut oil to fuel their vehicles when cut off from oil supplies. However, academic interest in straight vegetable oil declined in the 1980s due to falling petroleum prices and increased focus on biodiesel, which requires fewer vehicle modifications. While engineers and enthusiasts have experimented with vegetable oil as a diesel engine fuel since 1900, only one peer-reviewed study has compared the long-term effects of vegetable oil and 2 diesel fuel on engine wear. This study found no significant difference in engine deterioration for a specific engine model, the German Deutz F3L912W. Most diesel car engines can run on SVO or pure plant oil (PPO) with appropriate modifications, such as preheating the oil to reduce its viscosity. Preheating is typically achieved using engine heat or electricity. Without preheating, poor atomization, incomplete combustion, and carbonization can occur. A common solution for using SVO/PPO involves adding a secondary fuel tank for diesel fuel (petrodiesel or biodiesel) and a three-way valve to switch between the tanks. The engine is started on diesel, switched to vegetable oil once warmed up, and switched back to diesel before shutting off to prevent vegetable oil from solidifying in the engine or fuel lines during cold starts. In colder climates, additional heating of the vegetable oil fuel lines and tank is often necessary to prevent the oil from becoming too viscous or solidifying. Single-tank conversions have been attempted but often result in significant contamination of the engine’s lubrication oil due to blow-by during warm-up. While these systems may function in warm climates with indirect injection (IDI) engines, they are generally unsuitable for most other applications. For unmodified engines, blending SVO with diesel fuel can mitigate some adverse effects, but opinions on the effectiveness of this approach vary. Mechanics working with WVO have reported higher rates of wear and failure in fuel pumps and piston rings due to carbonization from partially combusted oil droplets. For standard use without blending or modifications, vegetable oil must be transesterified into biodiesel. Many cars with indirect injection engines and inline or mechanical Bosch injection pumps can run on pure SVO in all but winter temperatures. Turbo diesel engines tend to perform better due to increased injector pressure. Pre-CDI Mercedes-Benz vehicles and cars with PSA XUD engines also perform well, particularly as the latter often includes a coolant-heated fuel filter. In the UK, rapeseed oil (canola oil in the US and Canada) is the primary form of SVO used, with a freezing point of -10°C. Sunflower oil, which freezes at -17°C, is being investigated for improved cold-weather performance. However, oils with lower gelling points are less saturated and more prone to polymerization in the presence of oxygen. Coconut oil, palm oil, and animal fats like lard and tallow have high cetane numbers (indicating good combustion quality) and low iodine numbers (indicating resistance to polymerization). Some Pacific island nations use coconut oil as fuel to reduce costs and dependence on imported fuels while stabilizing the coconut oil market. Coconut oil is only viable in temperatures above 17°C unless two-tank systems or other heating accessories are used. Techniques developed for using oils like canola in cold climates can also be applied to make coconut oil usable at lower temperatures. Most residential furnaces and boilers designed for 2 heating oil can be modified to burn biodiesel or filtered, preheated waste vegetable oil. While these fuels are not as clean-burning as petroleum-based heating oil, they can offer significant cost savings if processed at home. Many restaurants provide used cooking oil for free or at minimal cost, and converting it to biodiesel is relatively simple and inexpensive. Burning filtered WVO directly is more challenging due to its viscosity but can be achieved with adequate preheating. In 2000, the United States produced over 11 billion liters of waste vegetable oil annually, primarily from industrial deep fryers in food processing plants and restaurants. If all this oil were collected and used as fuel, it could offset nearly 1% of US oil consumption. However, waste vegetable oil as fuel competes with other established uses. Pure plant oil (PPO) is not a byproduct of other industries and is limited only by the agricultural capacity of a given economy. For example, the UK exported 280,000 tonnes of rapeseed in 2005. Using set-aside land, the UK could meet its 5% biofuel target without importing environmentally damaging oil crops. In the US, converting an engine to burn vegetable oil is not legal under Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) guidelines, although no fines have been issued. Legal changes or a certification process may be required for vegetable oil conversions to gain popularity. Taxation on SVO as road fuel varies by country. Germany, for instance, offered 0% taxation but introduced a tax of €0.09 per liter in 2008, rising to €0.45 per liter by 2012. In the UK, SVO use is legal once fuel duty is paid, but drivers have been prosecuted for failing to do so. Recent changes in UK regulations exempt users of less than 2,500 liters per year from registration and duty payments. The interpretation of SVO as a fuel substitute rather than biodiesel by UK authorities has led to higher taxation rates, discouraging its use despite environmental benefits. This policy has been challenged by the SVO industry, with the UK Pure Plant Oil Association (UKPPOA) lobbying for legislative changes.
